title: Testing One Protein in a Foreign Cell
endLine: A foreign cell tests what one protein can do, not animal need.

scenes.tts: How do you test one protein inside a crowded cell? Copy its gene and put it into a foreign cell that normally lacks it. Let the host build it, then watch what response appears. That method is heterologous expression.
scenes.caption: How do you test one protein inside a crowded cell? Copy its gene and put it into a foreign cell that normally lacks it. Let the host build it, then watch what response appears. That method is heterologous expression.
scenes.visual: A crowded native cell fills over 60% of frame height, its membrane packed with many differently coloured geometric shapes (no molecular structures). One glowing teal gene strip lifts out and arcs into a smooth, empty host cell on the right; a single matching teal block settles into the host membrane while gentle ambient particles drift in both cells.
scenes.narration: How do you test one protein inside a crowded cell? Copy its gene and put it into a foreign cell that normally lacks it. Let the host build it, then watch what response appears. That method is heterologous expression.

scenes.visual: The host cell with its single teal membrane block centers smoothly with slow ambient drift while the title 'Testing One Protein in a Foreign Cell' appears cleanly above it in large high-contrast type, then fades.

scenes.tts: Heterologous simply means foreign. You make a D N A copy of an expressed gene, called c D N A. Or you start directly with its R N A. Then you deliver those instructions into a host cell lacking that response. Common hosts are cultured H E K two ninety-three cells and frog Xenopus oocytes.
scenes.caption: Heterologous simply means foreign. You make a DNA copy of an expressed gene, called cDNA. Or you start directly with its RNA. Then you deliver those instructions into a host cell lacking that response. Common hosts are cultured HEK293 cells and frog Xenopus oocytes.
scenes.visual: From the same stage, the glowing teal gene strip splits into two labelled instruction strands, 'cDNA' and 'RNA', that travel into two host cells shown side by side: a smaller cultured cell labelled 'HEK293' on the left and a larger round frog egg labelled 'Xenopus oocyte' on the right, each with a smooth membrane and slow drifting dots inside.
scenes.narration: Heterologous simply means foreign. You make a DNA copy of an expressed gene, called cDNA. Or you start directly with its RNA. Then you deliver those instructions into a host cell lacking that response. Common hosts are cultured HEK293 cells and frog Xenopus oocytes.

scenes.tts: The host builds the protein and puts it in its membrane. Now add a stimulus, and compare with an untransfected cell carrying no added gene. The control trace stays flat, while the test cell responds. Heterologous expression tests molecular sufficiency: whether one protein, in a foreign cell, produces a response.
scenes.caption: The host builds the protein and puts it in its membrane. Now add a stimulus, and compare with an untransfected cell carrying no added gene. The control trace stays flat, while the test cell responds. Heterologous expression tests molecular sufficiency: whether one protein, in a foreign cell, produces a response.
scenes.visual: Split view of the same host cell world: left is an 'Untransfected control' cell with an empty membrane; right is the 'Test cell' as teal blocks appear in its membrane. Amber stimulus dots drift across both cells. Below each cell, a schematic response trace draws live: flat on the left, jumping upward on the right, under a crisp label 'Molecular sufficiency'.

The control trace stays flat, while the test cell responds. Heterologous expression tests molecular sufficiency: whether one protein, in a foreign cell, produces a response.

scenes.tts: Now test a classic trap. You inject R N A for an unknown membrane protein into frog oocytes, and chloride current appears. Water-injected oocytes from the same frog stay flat. Does that prove your protein is itself a chloride channel?
scenes.caption: Now test a classic trap. You inject RNA for an unknown membrane protein into frog oocytes, and chloride current appears. Water-injected oocytes from the same frog stay flat. Does that prove your protein is itself a chloride channel?
scenes.visual: The split host cells enlarge into two frog oocytes: 'Water control' on the left and 'RNA-injected' on the right, with glass needles injecting water on the left and an RNA strand on the right. Below them, a schematic chloride-current trace stays flat for the water control and rises sharply for the RNA-injected oocyte. Bold text appears: 'Is your protein the chloride channel?'
scenes.narration: Now test a classic trap. You inject RNA for an unknown membrane protein into frog oocytes, and chloride current appears. Water-injected oocytes from the same frog stay flat. Does that prove your protein is itself a chloride channel?

scenes.visual: Hold the two frog oocytes, the flat water-control schematic trace, the rising RNA-injected schematic trace, and the question 'Is your protein the chloride channel?' while a subtle glowing countdown ring rotates steadily for 4.5 seconds.

scenes.tts: Not yet. Oocytes carry chloride channels of their own, and foreign proteins can switch them on. Good experiments include water-injected or untransfected controls, and match surface expression. Otherwise, different amounts alone can mislead. To show one protein is enough to form the pathway, purify it into a lipid bilayer with no other proteins.

scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly onto the RNA-injected oocyte membrane: faint dormant pale-blue native chloride pores flicker open as foreign teal blocks accumulate nearby. Then pull back to paired test and control cells with a schematic 'Surface level' bar gauge equalizing both sides. Finally, one isolated teal block lifts out into a clean double-line 'Lipid bilayer' with no other shapes and passes a clean ion pulse.

scenes.tts: Two limits keep results honest. First, no current above background does not tell you why. A mutant protein may be absent, mislocalized, or unable to conduct. Second, a response in a foreign cell shows only sufficiency. Testing whether an intact animal needs the gene requires removing it there.

scenes.visual: Two panels evolving from the same cell stage. Left ('No current', with a flat schematic trace): the cell cycles cleanly through three states for a mutant protein — empty cell ('Absent'), teal blocks trapped inside the interior ('Mislocalized'), and a plugged membrane block ('No conduction'). Right: the responding foreign cell sits beside the silhouette of an intact animal marked with a question mark over the gene.

scenes.tts: Even so, the method unlocked major discoveries. In 1997, Caterina, Julius and colleagues put pools of rodent sensory-neuron genes into H E K cells. They watched for calcium entering when they added capsaicin, the chilli burn. Splitting a responding pool left one gene: T R P V one. In those foreign cells, its channel also opened above about forty-three degrees Celsius.
scenes.caption: Even so, the method unlocked major discoveries. In 1997, Caterina, Julius and colleagues put pools of rodent sensory-neuron genes into HEK cells. They watched for calcium entering when they added capsaicin, the chilli burn. Splitting a responding pool left one gene: TRPV1. In those foreign cells, its channel also opened above about 43 °C.
scenes.visual: Return to the HEK host cell stage, labelled '1997': rows of tiny cDNA pool tubes; the responding pool splits again and again, narrowing to one glowing orange strand labelled 'TRPV1' entering the HEK cell membrane. Adding 'Capsaicin' drops triggers bright calcium dots streaming in and a jumping schematic calcium trace; then a schematic temperature gauge rises past '43 °C' and opens the same orange channel block again.
scenes.narration: Even so, the method unlocked major discoveries. In 1997, Caterina, Julius and colleagues put pools of rodent sensory-neuron genes into HEK cells. They watched for calcium entering when they added capsaicin, the chilli burn. Splitting a responding pool left one gene: TRPV1. In those foreign cells, its channel also opened above about 43 °C.

scenes.tts: In 2006, Suh, Inoue, Meyer and Hille expressed potassium channels in foreign cells. Depleting one membrane lipid, P I P two, made the current fall, so lipid loss alone was enough. In 2020, Shui and colleagues paired Xenopus oocytes carrying two worm junction proteins, called innexins. Current strongly favoured one direction between the cells.
scenes.caption: In 2006, Suh, Inoue, Meyer and Hille expressed potassium channels in foreign cells. Depleting one membrane lipid, PIP2, made the current fall, so lipid loss alone was enough. In 2020, Shui and colleagues paired Xenopus oocytes carrying two worm junction proteins, called innexins. Current strongly favoured one direction between the cells.
scenes.visual: Two beats on the same host-cell stage. First ('2006'): a foreign cell with teal potassium channel blocks ('KCNQ2/KCNQ3') and amber inner-membrane markers ('PIP2'); as the amber markers fade away, the teal blocks shut and a schematic current trace falls. Second ('2020'): two Xenopus oocytes touch, labelled 'UNC-9' (left) and 'UNC-7b' (right), bridged by innexin junction bars; a bold animated current arrow flows from UNC-9 to UNC-7b while reverse flow is blocked.

scenes.tts: Moving one gene into a foreign cell strips away the crowd. With careful controls, it reveals what one protein can do on its own. Whether an intact animal needs it takes a different test.
scenes.caption: Moving one gene into a foreign cell strips away the crowd. With careful controls, it reveals what one protein can do on its own. Whether an intact animal needs it takes a different test.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the opening world: the crowded native cell dims softly into the background while the clean foreign host cell with its single glowing protein and paired flat control cell stand sharp in the foreground, alongside the faint silhouette of an intact animal with an open question mark.
